respuestas.q: Should women train differently from men?

r.t: There is no need: with the same training, the evidence points to women and men gaining muscle in similar proportions, so the programme can be the same. What changes is the starting point, not the response to training.
p: Pooling 29 studies in adults aged 18 to 45, the relative gain in muscle was practically the same in women and men.
Men gain slightly more in absolute terms, in the upper body and not the lower body, probably because they start with more muscle mass.
In people over 50, in 30 studies, women even gained slightly more relative strength in the legs.
To track your progress, compare yourself with yourself, as a percentage improvement, not with other people.
r.n: What does change the guidance is age or a situation such as pregnancy, not sex; the data are from adults.

respuestas.q: Should I adapt my training to my menstrual cycle?

r.t: You do not need a phase-by-phase calendar: the cycle seems to change performance little and there is no basis for general rules. Adjust each session to how you feel that day.
p: A pooled analysis of studies found a trivial effect on performance at the start of the cycle (the early follicular phase), with low-quality evidence.
A review of reviews considers it premature to conclude that cycle hormones change gains in strength or muscle.
With oral contraceptives, performance might on average be slightly lower than with a natural cycle, but the difference is very probably trivial.
If your period causes you pain or tiredness, lower the intensity that day or change exercise: it is your decision, not a rule.
r.c: If you train a lot and your periods stop for several cycles in a row, do not assume it is normal: see your doctor.
r.n: Many studies on the cycle are of low quality and inconsistent: the conclusion could change with better studies.

f.leido: indicated a trivial effect […] with reduced exercise performance observed in the early follicular phase […] The quality of evidence for this review was classified as “low” […] general guidelines on exercise performance across the MC cannot be formed […] a personalised approach should be taken

respuestas.q: I train a lot and my periods have stopped: is that normal?

r.t: It is best not to assume it is normal: losing your period for several cycles in a row can be a sign of relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs), in other words, not enough energy for the training you do.

respuestas.q: I’m pregnant: can I exercise?

r.t: Yes, and it is recommended: if there is no medical reason not to, the WHO advises regular physical activity during pregnancy and after giving birth, at least 150 minutes a week of moderate intensity, with aerobic and strengthening exercises.
p: Adding gentle stretching may also help, according to the WHO.
On an effort scale of 0 to 10, moderate is usually a 5 or a 6.
If you plan to compete or to do much more than recommended, do so under the supervision of a specialist health professional.
In Tenerife, bear the heat in mind: the WHO advises avoiding activity in excessive heat, especially when humidity is high.
r.c: Stop and seek advice straight away if you have vaginal bleeding, a continuous loss of fluid from the vagina, regular and painful contractions, or breathlessness or dizziness that does not ease with rest. With severe chest pain, call 112.
r.n: The medical reasons not to exercise are not listed here: the professional caring for you assesses them.

respuestas.q: Does exercise help prevent falls?

r.t: Yes: in older people living at home, exercise reduces falls by about a quarter (23%), according to a Cochrane review of 108 trials, with high certainty.
p: What works most clearly is balance and functional exercises (everyday movements); combining several types probably does too, and tai chi might help.

For strength training alone, dancing or walking, there is not enough evidence to know whether they reduce falls.
The WHO asks people over 65 to do varied activity with balance and strength on at least 3 days a week, also to prevent falls.
r.c: If you have already fallen or are afraid of falling, ask your doctor or physiotherapist for a tailored programme.
r.n: As for fractures, exercise might reduce them, but that evidence is less firm and more studies are needed.

respuestas.q: Do I need to see a doctor before I start exercising?

There is a questionnaire to help you decide, the PAR-Q+; use it in full, in its official version.

respuestas.q: How do I know if exercise is moderate or vigorous?

r.t: Rate your effort from 0 to 10 according to your own capacity: for the WHO, moderate activity is usually a 5 or 6, vigorous a 7 or 8, and light from 2 to 4.
p: The talk test, from the US guidelines (2018): at a moderate pace you can talk, but not sing.
At a vigorous pace you cannot say more than a few words without stopping for breath.
It is a relative scale: the same walk can be moderate for one person and vigorous for another.
There is also an absolute scale in METs (multiples of the energy used at rest): moderate from 3 to less than 6, vigorous from 6.

respuestas.q: Do I have to walk 10,000 steps a day?

r.t: No. The 10,000 steps are not an official recommendation: a 2025 meta-analysis calls them an «unofficial» target without a clear basis. More steps are linked to lower risk, up to a point.

respuestas.q: Does walking count as exercise?

r.t: Yes: walking at a brisk pace is moderate aerobic activity and adds to the weekly minutes the WHO asks for (150 to 300 in adults). Strength training is separate.
p: Walking at a moderate pace uses 3.8 METs (multiples of the energy used at rest), and at a fast pace, 4.8: the WHO calls 3 to less than 6 moderate.
Uphill counts even more: walking up slopes of 6 to 10% equals 7 METs, already in the vigorous range (6 or more).
Walking does not replace strength training: the WHO separately asks for exercises for all the major groups, at least 2 days a week if you are an adult.
In the heat, walk in the cooler hours: the Spanish Ministry of Health advises avoiding outdoor sport in the middle of the day.
r.n: METs are average values for adults: they do not measure each person’s actual energy use.

respuestas.q: How should I breathe when lifting weights?

r.t: Breathe steadily and do not hold your breath during the effort: holding it while the muscle contracts (the Valsalva manoeuvre) is linked to a bigger rise in blood pressure.

respuestas.q: What is muscle soreness after exercise (DOMS) and how long does it last?

r.t: It is the pain and stiffness that appear hours after exercise you are not used to; it is worst on the second day and usually goes away on its own in less than a week.
p: It starts 6 to 12 hours after the effort and usually lasts 2 or 3 days.
It is caused mainly by new exercises or ones with a lot of braking (eccentric exercises, in which the muscle lengthens), such as walking downhill.
It is not caused by lactic acid, an idea that research does not confirm: it is due to inflammation of the muscle damaged by the effort.
To get less of it, progress gradually; doing the same exercise gently beforehand also protects you.
r.c: If it started with a sharp, sudden pain in one specific spot, or there is swelling, it may be an injury: seek advice.
r.n: The times of 6–12 hours, the second day and the 2–3 days come from a review focused on skiing.

respuestas.q: How can I tell muscle soreness from an injury?

r.t: Soreness appears hours later, as a stiff ache in the muscle you worked; an injury usually starts suddenly during the effort, with a sharp pain in one specific spot, sometimes with a snap.
p: Soreness: it comes hours later, the muscle is stiff and a little weak, it may hurt at rest and it gets better on its own over a few days.
Muscle tear: sharp, sudden pain, a feeling of something snapping and pain in a well-defined spot.
Other signs of injury: large or growing swelling or bruising, difficulty moving it or being unable to put weight on it. If it is an injury, stop exercising.
r.c: Call 112 or go to an emergency department if you heard a snap, the area is deformed, numb or tingling, or the skin looks bluish, grey or cold.
r.n: These clues are a guide, not a diagnosis: if the pain is very severe, gets worse or does not improve, have a doctor or physiotherapist assess it.

respuestas.q: I have high blood pressure: can I lift weights?

r.t: Yes, in general: with your blood pressure under control, low- to moderate-intensity strength training is safe if you breathe properly, and it helps lower it. If your blood pressure is poorly controlled, talk to your doctor first.
p: Do not hold your breath during strength training; breathe steadily: holding your breath raises blood pressure more.
The European guideline (2020) calls for at least 30 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise 5 to 7 days a week, and strength training on 2 or 3.
In people with high blood pressure, strength training lowered resting blood pressure by about 6 mmHg systolic and 5 diastolic (AHA, 2023).
If you take blood pressure medication, make your cool-down longer to avoid a drop in blood pressure.
r.c: See your doctor before starting, as the American Heart Association asks; with a resting systolic pressure above 160 mmHg, the European guideline considers it poorly controlled.

r.t: Exercise is recommended, but if you use insulin or tablets that make your body produce more insulin, your blood sugar can drop during exercise or long afterwards: check your glucose beforehand and talk to your care team.

respuestas.q: I have back pain: can I train?

r.t: In general, yes: with low back pain, staying active and doing gentle exercise within the limits of the pain can help you recover sooner. Avoid spending the day in bed.
p: If something hurts a little more when you exercise, it should settle within 20 or 30 minutes of finishing.
Move gently every 30 or 40 minutes: people who avoid normal movement too much are more likely to have pain that lasts longer.
See your doctor if it does not improve within a few weeks or stops you getting on with daily life, and straight away if you feel unwell, with chills, or the pain is severe and sudden.
If the pain began after a serious accident, fall or blow, call 112.
r.c: Call 112 if you have pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in both legs; lose feeling around your genitals or anus; notice changes when urinating, when opening your bowels or during sex, or have chest pain.

respuestas.q: I’ve been injured: when can I go back to training?

r.t: It depends on the injury. With sprains and strains, after 1 to 3 days of protection, it is best to start moving and loading the area again gradually, with pain as your guide; intense effort comes later.
p: Sprain or strain: most get better in about 2 weeks, but avoid running and other intense effort for up to 8 weeks; a severe one can take months (NHS).
An editorial (BJSM, 2020) calls for keeping rest to a minimum, starting pain-free aerobic exercise after a few days and letting pain set the pace.
After a concussion, the return to sport follows 6 steps that usually take at least 24 hours each: one week at the very least.
r.c: See a physiotherapist or your doctor if it does not improve, if the pain is very severe or getting worse, or if you cannot put weight on it; after a blow to the head, always before going back.

respuestas.q: My knees hurt when I come down a mountain: what should I do?

r.t: Going downhill puts a lot of load on the knee. Use poles and go down calmly. If the pain does not improve or the knee swells, get it checked.

r.c: Call 112 or go to the emergency department if you heard a crack, the knee has changed shape or it feels numb. Get it checked if you cannot put weight on it, it is very swollen or it does not improve with care.

respuestas.q: How do I recognise heatstroke?

respuestas.q: How much water should I drink when I exercise in the heat?

r.t: In the heat, the Spanish Ministry of Health asks you to drink often, even if you are not thirsty. When training, the amount depends on how much you sweat: there is no fixed figure.
p: Beforehand, 5 to 10 ml per kilo of body weight 2 to 4 hours before: about 350 to 700 ml if you weigh 70 kg.
Adjust to how much you sweat: each kilo you lose while training is roughly a litre of sweat, and it is best not to lose more than 2% of your body weight.
In long efforts, be guided by your thirst, which also warns you in the heat, and do not drink more than you sweat. If you gain weight while training, you are drinking too much.
r.c: Call 112 if, after a long effort during which you drank a lot, you get a headache, vomiting or confusion: there may be too little sodium in your blood.
r.n: The per-kilo figures come from a position statement for athletes: it has not been confirmed that they apply to children and teenagers.

r.t: Given how you walk in the mountains, it makes sense to strengthen the quadriceps, glutes and hips, calves and shins, and abs and lower back. No trial has been found that proves this in hikers.

respuestas.q: Will strength training make me a better runner?

r.t: Probably yes: in a meta-analysis of 31 studies with 652 runners, strength training with heavy loads slightly improved running economy (the energy you use to keep up a pace), with moderate certainty.
p: Heavy loads are 80% or more of what you can lift once; the improvements came with 2–4 days a week for 6–14 weeks.
Those studies used, for example, half squats, leg presses and deadlifts.
Jumps (plyometrics) only improved economy at paces of 5:00 min/km or slower; combining methods gave more improvement, but with low certainty.
In high-level runners, 2–3 sessions a week for 8–12 weeks gave a large improvement, in a smaller meta-analysis.
r.n: The studies are of middle- and long-distance runners, with few women (180 of 652).

respuestas.q: What can I do on the plane to look after my legs?

r.t: On flights of more than 4 hours, get up and walk around from time to time and move your calves in your seat. On shorter flights, the risk of thrombosis (a clot in a vein) is negligible.
p: To move them, raise and lower your heels and the tips of your feet several times.
Higher risk: active cancer, oestrogen (contraceptives or hormone therapy), recent surgery or injury, pregnancy or the postnatal period, previous thrombosis, obesity or being over 40.
If you are at higher risk, ask for an aisle seat and ask your doctor about compression stockings; aspirin is not generally recommended for this.
Drinking water is reasonable, but it has not been shown to prevent travellers’ thrombosis.
r.c: Call 112 if you suddenly become short of breath, have chest pain when breathing or faint. If a leg is swollen, painful, warm or red, get it checked soon.

respuestas.q: How can I cope better with jet lag when I arrive?

r.t: Use light: if you have flown east, seek bright light early in the morning and avoid it in the late afternoon and evening; if you have flown west, avoid strong light early in the morning.
p: Jet lag appears when you cross at least two time zones. On average, the body adjusts by 1 hour a day when travelling east and 1.5 when travelling west.
If you need to sleep during the day, keep naps short, 20 to 30 minutes: long ones can stop you sleeping at night.
A few days before, move your bedtime by one hour a day: earlier if you are travelling east, later if you are going west.
Avoid too much alcohol: it helps you fall asleep sooner, but it disrupts your sleep more.
r.n: The CDC does not give a time for exercise; training outdoors at the time of light that suits you is reasoning, not a guideline.
